title: Conservatorships: #freebritney
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant (with guest producer Dave Kustin) examine conservatorships, using the Britney Spears case as the entry point. They cover what a conservatorship is, how guardianship and conservatorship terms differ by state, the types (financial, physical, general, limited), durations (short-term, temporary, permanent), the legal tests for imposing one, California conservatee rights, the Spears case allegations and disputed facts, conservator pay (including Jamie Spears and Andrew Wallet), a GAO report on weak oversight, and proposed federal legislation to make it easier to end conservatorships. The episode closes with a listener email about the knocker-upper job and a sign-off.

entities.name: Free Act (Freedom and Right to Emancipate from Exploitation Act)

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to conservatorships
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the episode and set up the topic as a dry legal subject prompted by the Britney Spears situation, noting how such cases recall old-fashioned claims that a family member is 'crazy.'

segments.title: Britney Spears background and what a conservatorship is
segments.summary: They give background on Spears's 2008 public troubles, hospitalizations and the conservatorship her father Jamie Spears leads. They define conservatorship as one person being legally in charge of another's decisions, note state differences between guardianship and conservatorship, and describe the court petition, evaluation and hearing process. They say Spears was reportedly not informed beforehand and had a court-appointed lawyer.

segments.title: Disputed facts of the Spears conservatorship
segments.summary: The hosts discuss conflicting accounts of how the 2008 conservatorship was granted, including a claim that the process lasted about ten minutes and the judge's denial of any back-room deal. They mention a New Yorker article and a documentary, and the hosts note that Spears was held in psychiatric holds before the petition.

segments.title: Types of conservatorship: financial, physical, general, limited
segments.summary: The hosts explain financial, physical, general and limited conservatorships. Limited conservatorship is the most common goal, with the aim of restricting as little as possible. Spears's case is described as involving her father controlling finances, health and career, with his reported share of her earnings and the threat of visitation with her children used as leverage.

segments.title: Duration: short-term, temporary and permanent conservatorships
segments.summary: They distinguish short-term conservatorships (typically under ninety days, often for rehab or immediate needs), temporary ones that can become permanent, and permanent ones, which are the most typical and can be removed by petition.

segments.title: Legal tests for conservatorship and the case for and against
segments.summary: The hosts describe the two-pronged test: whether a person cannot meet basic needs, or cannot make sound financial decisions. They note conservatorship is usually tied to incapacity such as dementia, Alzheimer's, a coma or lifelong disability. They also argue the case should be viewed with an open mind, since sealed court records make it hard to know the truth and defenders say the arrangement helped Spears's finances.

segments.title: California conservatee rights and Spears's claims
segments.summary: The hosts cover rights listed in the Judicial Council of California's handbook for conservatees, including receiving salary, allowance, receiving mail, marrying, changing a will and hiring one's own lawyer. They discuss Spears's claims that her father restricts dating, marriage and an IUD removal, and her court-appointed lawyer.

segments.title: Conservator pay, oversight failures and the GAO report
segments.summary: They discuss conservator pay (between forty and a hundred dollars an hour), Jamie Spears's reported compensation, and co-conservator Andrew Wallet's request for a salary of about four million dollars a year, which led to his removal. They describe the requirement to keep detailed financial records, and a GAO report in which investigators got conservatorships approved for fictitious identities in four states without background checks.

segments.title: Ending conservatorships and the proposed Free Act
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how a conservatorship is ended, noting that current law requires proof of fraud or abuse. They describe proposed federal legislation co-sponsored by Representatives Charlie Crist and Nancy Mace, the Free Act, which would allow removal without abuse or fraud and mirrors a 2019 bill that stalled. They debate the individual's right to choose versus protecting people from harmful influence, and discuss Spears's wish for an attorney of her choosing.

segments.title: Listener mail: knocker-upper and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener from Dublin writes about his great-grandfather, a knocker-upper who woke workers before alarm clocks were common. The hosts share a short anecdote and sign off, pointing listeners to the email address and a shout-out to comedians Babs Gray and Tess Barker.
